document_sections.heading: Executive summary of recommendations
document_sections.content: The summary presents recommendations on diagnosing and managing tubal, cervical, caesarean scar, interstitial, cornual, ovarian, abdominal and heterotopic pregnancy. The recommendations are detailed under the diagnostic, management, fertility, counselling, service and training headings below. Their letter grades denote recommendation grades, not evidence levels.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy
document_sections.content: For tubal pregnancy, transvaginal ultrasound is preferred for diagnosis (B), and clinicians should seek an adnexal mass that moves independently of the ovary (D). Serum progesterone does not help predict ectopic pregnancy (B); serum beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin (b-hCG) helps plan care after ultrasound has shown one (C). Cervical pregnancy may be identified by an empty uterine cavity, a barrel-shaped cervix, a sac below the internal cervical os, an absent ‘sliding sign’ and perisac blood flow on colour Doppler (D); obtain serum b-hCG once at diagnosis (D). For caesarean scar pregnancy, ultrasound is the principal investigation: use transvaginal imaging, adding transabdominal imaging if necessary (D). Described transvaginal criteria may aid diagnosis (D), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may serve as a second-line test when findings are equivocal and local diagnostic expertise exists (D). Routine biochemical tests are unnecessary. Interstitial pregnancy may be identified by an empty cavity, a laterally located sac or conception products in the intramural tube with less than 5 mm of surrounding myometrium in every imaging plane, and an ‘interstitial line sign’ (D). Where available, three-dimensional ultrasound can corroborate two-dimensional findings and help distinguish early intrauterine or angular pregnancy (D); MRI may also help (D). Measure serum b-hCG at diagnosis to inform care and, in some cases, repeat it in 48 hours. For cornual pregnancy, suggested ultrasound findings are a single interstitial tubal segment in the principal uterine body, a mobile sac or conception products separate from the uterus but completely enclosed by myometrium, and a vascular pedicle linking the sac to the unicornuate uterus (D). Obtain one serum b-hCG measurement for management planning; a repeat in 48 hours can sometimes assist. No agreed ultrasound criteria specifically diagnose ovarian pregnancy (D); obtain serum b-hCG once and consider a repeat in 48 hours when useful for management. Defined ultrasound findings can aid abdominal-pregnancy diagnosis (D); MRI can additionally help diagnose advanced disease and plan surgery (D). Suspicion rests on elevated serum b-hCG together with ultrasound findings (D). Ultrasound establishes heterotopic pregnancy by showing both an intrauterine and an ectopic pregnancy (D); serum b-hCG has limited diagnostic utility (D).

document_sections.heading: Management options
document_sections.content: For tubal pregnancy, laparoscopy is preferred to open surgery (A). With a healthy opposite tube, salpingectomy is preferred to salpingotomy (B); consider salpingotomy when prior ectopic pregnancy, contralateral tubal damage, earlier abdominal surgery or previous pelvic inflammatory disease may impair fertility (C). After salpingotomy, explain persistent-trophoblast risk, the need for serum b-hCG surveillance and the small possibility of further systemic methotrexate or salpingectomy (good practice point). Suitable women may be offered systemic methotrexate; do not give it at the initial visit unless ectopic pregnancy is unequivocally diagnosed and viable intrauterine pregnancy excluded (B). Expectant care is possible in clinically stable women with ultrasound-confirmed ectopic pregnancy and declining b-hCG initially less than 1500 iu/l (B). For cervical pregnancy, methotrexate can be considered (D); because surgical approaches have high failure rates, reserve them for life-threatening haemorrhage (D). Counsel women with caesarean scar pregnancy about serious maternal morbidity and mortality (D). In the first trimester, consider medical or surgical treatment, with or without supplementary haemostatic measures (D). Evidence cannot establish a preferred individual intervention, although existing literature favours surgery over medicine for effectiveness (D). Stable interstitial pregnancy can be managed without surgery (D); expectant care is appropriate only with low or substantially falling b-hCG when adding methotrexate may not improve outcome (D). Methotrexate is effective, but evidence does not favour local over systemic administration (D). Laparoscopic cornual resection or salpingotomy is effective (D), and hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic or ultrasound guidance may be considered (D). Evidence on future-pregnancy safety and complications does not support recommending other nonsurgical techniques (D). Excise the rudimentary horn in cornual pregnancy by laparoscopy or laparotomy (D). If ovarian pregnancy requires diagnostic laparoscopy, definitive surgery is preferred (D); systemic methotrexate can be used when surgical risk is high or after surgery for residual persistent trophoblast or persistently elevated b-hCG (D). Laparoscopic removal is an option for early abdominal pregnancy (D); systemic methotrexate combined with ultrasound-guided fetocide is a possible alternative (D). Manage advanced abdominal pregnancy by laparotomy (D). In heterotopic pregnancy, the intrauterine gestation must shape management (B). Consider methotrexate only if that gestation is nonviable or the woman does not wish to continue it (D). For clinically stable women, local potassium chloride or hyperosmolar glucose injection with sac aspiration is an option (D). Remove the ectopic pregnancy surgically when haemodynamically unstable; surgery is also an option when stable (D). Expectant care may be considered when ultrasound indicates a nonviable ectopic gestation (D).

document_sections.heading: Do rhesus D (RhD)-negative women with an ectopic pregnancy require anti-D immunoglobulin?
document_sections.content: Offer anti-D prophylaxis according to national protocol to RhD-negative women after surgical removal of ectopic pregnancy or when bleeding recurs, is heavy, or accompanies abdominal pain (D).

document_sections.heading: What are the long-term fertility prospects following an ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Counsel women without prior subfertility or tubal disease that the available management approaches do not differ in fertility rates, subsequent tubal ectopic-pregnancy risk or tubal patency (D). Explain to women with previous subfertility that expectant or medical management of tubal pregnancy is associated with better reproductive outcomes than radical surgery (C). Women treated with methotrexate for tubal pregnancy may be reassured that ovarian reserve is unaffected (D). After UAE and systemic methotrexate for nontubal ectopic pregnancy, advise that subsequent live births have been reported (D). Following laparoscopic treatment of ovarian pregnancy, advise that future fertility prospects are favourable (D).

document_sections.heading: What support and counselling should be offered to women undergoing treatment for ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Whenever feasible, discuss each treatment approach’s benefits and disadvantages and involve women fully in treatment selection (D). Explain access to patient organisations, including the Ectopic Pregnancy Trust, and local bereavement services (D). Muscle-relaxation training may benefit women receiving methotrexate (C). Recommend waiting at least 3 months after methotrexate before attempting conception (D).

document_sections.heading: Service and training
document_sections.content: Early-pregnancy services should offer assessment 7 days a week, direct access after referral from general practice or accident and emergency, diagnostic and treatment algorithms, transvaginal ultrasound, and serum b-hCG measurement. Women should be able to obtain all suitable treatments; where local provision is incomplete, establish explicit referral routes (good practice point). Surgery and diagnostic ultrasound require appropriately trained clinicians; laparoscopy also requires suitable equipment and trained operating-theatre personnel. Clinicians using ultrasound-guided needle techniques for medical treatment need specific training (good practice points). Experienced support must be available if a surgeon cannot perform the full range of procedures (good practice point). Virtual-reality simulation may be used to teach salpingectomy (D).

document_sections.heading: 1. Purpose and scope
document_sections.content: This evidence-based guidance addresses diagnosis and management of tubal, cervical, caesarean scar, interstitial, cornual, ovarian, abdominal and heterotopic ectopic pregnancies. It does not address diagnosis or management of pregnancy of unknown location (PUL); a National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline discusses that subject.

document_sections.heading: 2. Introduction and background epidemiology
document_sections.content: Ectopic pregnancy means implantation outside the endometrial cavity. In the UK, incidence is approximately 11/1000 pregnancies, with an estimated 11 000 diagnoses each year; among women attending early-pregnancy units, incidence is 2–3%. Six maternal deaths were reported between 2006 and 2008. The case-fatality rate has declined in recent years, suggesting that earlier identification and treatment may have contributed. Risk factors include tubal injury after infection or surgery, smoking and in vitro fertilisation, although the majority of affected women have no identifiable risk factor.

document_sections.heading: 3. Identification and assessment of evidence
document_sections.content: The guideline followed the standard methodology for Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) Green-top Guidelines. Searches covered MEDLINE, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library, restricting results to human studies in English published between 1995 and July 2015. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) were combined with keywords concerning ectopic-pregnancy locations, PUL and extrauterine pregnancy. Searches also covered the National Guideline Clearinghouse, NICE Evidence Search and Trip. Recommendations draw on available evidence where possible; evidence gaps are identified as ‘good practice points’ (GPP). Appendix I describes assessment and grading.

document_sections.heading: 4. Diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy
document_sections.content: Diagnosis is addressed separately for tubal, cervical, caesarean scar, interstitial, cornual, ovarian, abdominal and heterotopic pregnancy. The subsections distinguish imaging findings from the role of biochemical investigations.

document_sections.heading: 4.1 How is a tubal pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Transvaginal imaging provides the preferred diagnostic approach; serum b-hCG contributes to management planning after ultrasound visualisation, rather than independently establishing location.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Use transvaginal ultrasound to diagnose tubal ectopic pregnancy (B); where possible, identify it directly as an adnexal lesion moving separately from the ovary (D). Most tubal pregnancies should be visible by this method. Reported sensitivity for ectopic-pregnancy diagnosis is 87.0–99.0%, and specificity is 94.0–99.9% (Evidence level 2++). Most are seen at the first examination; initially unseen pregnancies are classified as PUL, but some are too early and small to be detectable rather than having been missed. Laparoscopy is no longer the diagnostic gold standard: false-negative results of 3.0–4.5% have been reported when performed too early (Evidence level 2++). An inhomogeneous or noncystic adnexal lesion occurs in around 50–60% of cases; an empty extrauterine sac in around 20–40%; and an extrauterine sac containing a yolk sac and/or embryonic pole, with or without cardiac activity, in around 15–20%. No endometrial appearance or thickness specifically supports tubal pregnancy. Fluid within the uterine cavity, termed a ‘pseudosac’, appears in up to 20% of cases; distinguishing it from an early intrauterine sac can be difficult. Intradesidual and double decidual signs support an early intrauterine gestation: respectively, an echogenic-rimmed fluid collection within thickened decidua on one side of the cavity, and an intrauterine collection enclosed by two concentric echogenic rings. A ‘pseudosac’ alone does not establish ectopic pregnancy; a small anechoic cystic structure is more likely to represent an early sac. One study found a 0.02% probability of ectopic pregnancy and a 99.98% probability of intrauterine pregnancy when a woman had a positive pregnancy test, a smooth-walled intrauterine anechoic cystic structure and no adnexal mass (Evidence level 3). Free fluid is common but not diagnostic: a little anechoic fluid in the pouch of Douglas can accompany either intrauterine or ectopic gestation. Echogenic fluid was reported in 28–56% of ectopic pregnancies; it may indicate rupture but more often reflects blood escaping from the tubal fimbrial end.

document_sections.heading: What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: For tubal pregnancy, serum progesterone cannot usefully predict ectopic pregnancy (B). Serum b-hCG helps plan management once ultrasound has visualised an ectopic pregnancy (C). A meta-analysis found that one b-hCG measurement cannot, by itself, predict ectopic pregnancy (Evidence level 1–). A low single value, such as less than 1000 iu/l, does not make ectopic pregnancy unlikely: many cases have levels below that threshold (Evidence level 2+). In an ultrasound-visualised tubal pregnancy, the initial serum b-hCG concentration is an important prognostic indicator for expectant and medical-management success (Evidence level 2–).

document_sections.heading: 4.2 How is a cervical pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Cervical pregnancy is uncommon, accounting for less than 1% of ectopic gestations. Defined ultrasound findings and a serum b-hCG measurement at diagnosis inform assessment and management.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: The following findings may support cervical-pregnancy diagnosis (D): an empty uterine cavity; barrel-shaped cervix; gestational sac below the internal cervical os; absent ‘sliding sign’; and colour-Doppler blood flow around the sac. The ‘sliding sign’ distinguishes an implanted cervical pregnancy from a miscarriage in the cervical canal: gentle probe pressure causes the sac to move along the endocervical canal in miscarriage, but not when implanted in the cervix (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Obtain a single serum b-hCG value at diagnosis (D). A measurement at ultrasound diagnosis can inform treatment selection. A value greater than 10 000 iu/l is associated with lower likelihood of successful methotrexate treatment (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.3 How is a caesarean scar pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Caesarean scar pregnancy is implantation into the myometrial defect at a previous uterine incision. Its estimated prevalence is approximately 1 in 2000 pregnancies. Such pregnancies can be potentially viable ongoing gestations or miscarriages located in the scar.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Ultrasound is the primary diagnostic method: use a transvaginal approach, supplemented by transabdominal imaging when needed (D). Published transvaginal criteria can assist (D): an empty uterine cavity; a gestational sac or solid trophoblastic mass anteriorly at the internal-os level within the earlier lower-segment caesarean scar; little or no myometrium between sac and bladder; prominent trophoblastic or placental Doppler vascularity; and an empty endocervical canal. MRI can be used second-line if findings remain equivocal and local expertise in interpreting scar pregnancies is available (D). Thirteen percent of reported scar pregnancies were initially labelled intrauterine or cervical. True prevalence may exceed reported estimates because some first-trimester miscarriages or terminations remain unidentified or unreported. Vial et al. described two proposed courses: growth toward the uterine cavity with potential viability but risk of massive implantation-site bleeding, or deeper progression toward the uterine serosa with potential first-trimester rupture and haemorrhage. Variable scar appearances and changing placental development further complicate diagnosis. The diagnostic criteria derive from descriptive case series and have not been validated; consequently, the guideline recommends regional-centre confirmation of suspected cases that are not emergencies to reduce false-positive diagnosis (Evidence level 3). MRI shows essentially the same features as ultrasound, but ultrasound is more accessible and less costly (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Do not routinely request biochemical investigations for diagnosing caesarean scar pregnancy (good practice point). Serum b-hCG has no diagnostic role here, although a baseline value may help if conservative treatment will be monitored.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 How is an interstitial pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Interstitial pregnancy implants in the interstitial segment of the fallopian tube. Reports place it at 1.0% to 6.3% of ectopic pregnancies. This tubal segment is about 1–2 cm long, passes through uterine-wall myometrium and opens into the uterine cavity at the tubal ostium (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.4.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Suggested diagnostic findings (D) are an empty uterine cavity; laterally situated conception products or sac within the interstitial intramural tube, covered by less than 5 mm of myometrium in every imaging plane; and an ‘interstitial line sign’. The line is a thin echogenic connection from the central uterine-cavity echo to the sac’s periphery; its reported sensitivity is 80% and specificity is 98% (Evidence level 3). Where available, three-dimensional ultrasound can corroborate two-dimensional findings and help avoid confusing interstitial pregnancy with early intrauterine or angular pregnancy, the latter implanting at a lateral uterine-cavity angle (D). A three-dimensional coronal view can show continuity between the endometrial cavity and interstitial tube. MRI can aid diagnosis (D): a sac-like structure lies lateral to the cornua within myometrium, and preservation of the junctional zone between cavity and structure adds support (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.4.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Measure serum b-hCG once at presentation when clinical features and ultrasound suggest interstitial pregnancy; this guides treatment rather than establishing diagnosis (good practice point). For some small ultrasound-identified lesions, repeating b-hCG in 48 hours may help choose treatment. Management decisions depend on clinical presentation, lesion size, fetal cardiac activity and b-hCG concentration; available paths include surgery, medication and observation.

document_sections.heading: 4.5 How is a cornual pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: An early description placed cornual pregnancy in one horn of a bicornuate uterus or one lateral half of a uterus tending to bifurcation. Some authors subsequently treated ‘interstitial’ and ‘cornual’ as interchangeable; others retained the definition involving a congenitally abnormal uterus (Evidence level 3). Under the latter definition, cornual pregnancy is the rarest ectopic form, with reported incidence of 1 in 76 000 pregnancies (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Suggested criteria (D) are visibility of a single interstitial tubal portion in the principal uterine body; a mobile gestational sac or conception products separate from the uterus yet entirely surrounded by myometrium; and a vascular pedicle connecting the sac with the unicornuate uterus (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: If symptoms and ultrasound suggest cornual pregnancy, obtain one serum b-hCG value to plan management; for some small sonographically identified pregnancies, repeat it in 48 hours if useful (good practice point). The decision among surgical, medical and expectant approaches depends on symptoms and other clinical findings, pregnancy size and serum b-hCG.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 How is an ovarian pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: A definitive preoperative diagnosis can be difficult. Suspicious ultrasound findings should prompt consideration of ovarian pregnancy; after surgery, histopathology confirms it (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.6.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: No specific agreed ultrasound diagnostic criteria exist (D). With an empty uterus, suggestive transvaginal findings include a broad echogenic ring enclosing an anechoic area on the ovary; a yolk sac or embryo is less often seen. Unlike a separate adnexal lesion, the structure or sac cannot be moved off the ovary by gentle palpation, yielding a negative sliding-organ sign. Identify the corpus luteum separately. Colour Doppler can help reveal a fetal heartbeat within the ovary. A complex echogenic adnexal lesion with pouch-of-Douglas fluid can indicate rupture (Evidence level 3). Corpus luteal cysts, a tubal pregnancy adherent to the ovary, a second corpus luteum, ovarian germ-cell tumours and other ovarian disorders can resemble it, so diagnosis is generally confirmed surgically and histologically.

document_sections.heading: 4.6.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Obtain a single serum b-hCG measurement at diagnosis for management planning; in some cases, another measurement in 48 hours may guide subsequent management (good practice point). Preoperative certainty may be difficult; suspicious ultrasound appearances warrant considering ovarian ectopic pregnancy. Postoperative histopathology establishes the diagnosis (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.7 How is an abdominal pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Defined ultrasound features can aid diagnosis (D). In advanced abdominal pregnancy, MRI can supplement diagnosis and inform the operative strategy (D).

document_sections.heading: 4.7.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Gerli et al. suggested four findings for early abdominal pregnancy: no intrauterine gestational sac; neither an obvious enlarged tube nor a complex adnexal lesion; a gestational cavity enclosed by bowel loops and separated from them by peritoneum; and marked sac mobility resembling fluctuation, especially when the transvaginal probe presses toward the posterior cul-de-sac. In a stable patient with ultrasound-confirmed or strongly suspected abdominal pregnancy, MRI can help verify location and identify placental attachment to vital structures, including major vessels or bowel. This can inform staffing, blood-product preparation, preoperative angiographic embolisation, bowel preparation and ureteral-catheter placement. Ultrasound and/or MRI may map placental position before laparotomy to help avoid incising it and causing uncontrollable bleeding (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.7.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Elevated serum b-hCG together with ultrasound findings raises suspicion of abdominal pregnancy (D). Early cases are usually found at laparoscopy undertaken to investigate persistently elevated serum b-hCG.

document_sections.heading: 4.8 How is heterotopic pregnancy diagnosed?
document_sections.content: Heterotopic pregnancy combines an intrauterine gestation with a simultaneous ectopic gestation. Ultrasound, rather than an isolated biochemical value, establishes their coexistence.

document_sections.heading: 4.8.1 What are the ultrasound criteria?
document_sections.content: Diagnosis requires ultrasound demonstration of an intrauterine pregnancy alongside an ectopic pregnancy (D). Consider this possibility after assisted reproductive technologies, with persistent pelvic pain despite a known intrauterine pregnancy, or when serum b-hCG remains high after miscarriage or termination (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.8.2 What biochemical investigations should be carried out?
document_sections.content: Serum b-hCG has limited diagnostic value (D). A value exceeding expectations for gestational age may prompt suspicion, although a complete or partial mole must also be considered. In a case series of 20 heterotopic pregnancies following assisted reproductive technology, mean b-hCG at pregnancy testing did not exceed that in nonheterotopic pregnancies (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 5. Management options
document_sections.content: Treatment choices depend on ectopic-pregnancy location, clinical stability, imaging, serum b-hCG where applicable, fertility considerations and, in heterotopic pregnancy, the status and desired outcome of the intrauterine gestation. The following subsections describe the location-specific options and their limitations.

document_sections.heading: 5.1 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for tubal pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Prefer laparoscopy to an open operation (A). When the contralateral tube is healthy, perform salpingectomy rather than salpingotomy (B). Consider salpingotomy if prior ectopic pregnancy, contralateral tubal damage, abdominal surgery or pelvic inflammatory disease has reduced fertility prospects (C). After salpingotomy, counsel about persistent trophoblast, serial serum b-hCG follow-up and the small possibility of subsequent systemic methotrexate or salpingectomy (good practice point). Systemic methotrexate may be offered to appropriately selected women, but not at their first visit unless ectopic pregnancy is unequivocal and a viable intrauterine gestation has been ruled out (B). Expectant management is an option for stable women with an ultrasound diagnosis and falling b-hCG initially less than 1500 iu/l (B).

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1 Surgical management
document_sections.content: Most tubal ectopic pregnancies receive surgery. Compared with laparotomy, laparoscopy has shorter operating time and hospital stay, less intraoperative blood loss, lower costs and analgesic needs, and fewer adhesions. Nevertheless, cited evidence found no difference in health benefits, including subsequent successful pregnancy, between these approaches. In a multicentre randomised controlled trial (RCT) of 446 women with laparoscopically verified tubal pregnancy and a healthy contralateral tube, cumulative ongoing pregnancy was 60.7% after salpingotomy versus 56.2% after salpingectomy. Persistent trophoblast affected 14 [7%] versus 1 [less than 1%], respectively (relative risk [RR] 15.0, 95% CI 2.0–113.4). Repeat ectopic pregnancy affected 18 women (8%) after salpingotomy and 12 (5%) after salpingectomy (RR 1.6, 95% CI 0.8–3.3). The investigators concluded that salpingotomy did not significantly improve fertility when the opposite tube was healthy (Evidence level 1+). Among women with fertility-reducing factors, one study found later intrauterine pregnancy in 75% after salpingotomy versus 40% after salpingectomy; without such factors, rates exceeded 90% in both groups (Evidence level 2–). Persistent trophoblast is indicated by b-hCG failing to decline as expected, principally after salpingotomy. Although levels can sometimes normalise without additional treatment, serial measurements allow identification of a plateau or rise for which methotrexate may be administered. NICE recommends serum b-hCG at 7 days after salpingotomy and weekly thereafter until negative (Evidence level 3). Studies report persistent trophoblast in 3.9–11.0% after salpingotomy. Proposed predictors include higher preoperative b-hCG, faster preoperative increase and larger tubal masses, but convincing evidence is absent and no definitive predictive factors are established.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2 Pharmacological management
document_sections.content: Methotrexate 50 mg/m2 as a single dose has commonly replaced repeat surgery for persistent trophoblast, without formal comparative studies. In one randomised trial, prophylactic methotrexate at laparoscopic salpingotomy reduced persistent trophoblast compared with salpingotomy alone (1.9% versus 14.5%; RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.02–0.97; Evidence level 1–). Systemic methotrexate is the drug most commonly used for tubal pregnancy; RCTs comparing it with laparoscopy found comparable success in selected cases (Evidence level 1–). Although multidose administration is possible, a single intramuscular dose of 50 mg/m2 is most common. Measure serum b-hCG on days 4 and 7 after treatment. If it falls by more than 15% between those days, continue weekly measurements until less than 15 iu/l. If it does not fall by 15%, consider repeat transvaginal ultrasound to check for ectopic fetal cardiac activity and substantial haemoperitoneum, followed by consideration of another methotrexate dose. Across reports, single-dose success ranges from 65–95%, and 3–27% need a second dose. Selection criteria differ: a review included studies of PUL or presumed, nonvisualised ectopic pregnancies and others with b-hCG already declining that would have resolved untreated. The largest cited single study, involving 559 ectopic-pregnancy cases, reported 90.7% (507/559) methotrexate success (Evidence level 3). Lower starting b-hCG predicts greater success: cited studies report 81–98% with levels less than 1000 iu/l versus 38% with levels greater than 5000 iu/l. A yolk sac, fetal pole or fetal cardiac activity significantly predicts failure, whereas success is greater without a visible sac. Smaller pretreatment b-hCG increases favour success; an increase of up to 11–20% over 48 hours before methotrexate was associated with higher success. Reported success was 88–100% when b-hCG fell from day 1 to day 4 after treatment, versus 42–62% when it rose. Advise avoidance of alcohol and folate-containing vitamins during methotrexate treatment. Reported adverse effects include marrow suppression, pulmonary fibrosis, nonspecific pneumonitis, liver cirrhosis, renal failure and gastric ulceration; the most common are excessive flatulence and bloating from intestinal gas, temporary mild liver-enzyme elevation and stomatitis. An appropriate candidate is haemodynamically stable, has low serum b-hCG—ideally less than 1500 iu/l but possibly up to 5000 iu/l—no sonographic fetal cardiac activity, certain exclusion of intrauterine pregnancy, willingness to attend follow-up and no known methotrexate sensitivity. NICE recommends first-line methotrexate for women able to return for follow-up who have no significant pain, an unruptured mass smaller than 35 mm without a visible heartbeat, serum b-hCG between 1500 and 5000 iu/l, and no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound (Evidence level 3). Before treatment, diagnosis must be correct. Because many ectopic pregnancies appear as inhomogeneous masses, repeating b-hCG in 48 hours is prudent in these cases: a decline may support observation, while a rise potentially compatible with viable intrauterine pregnancy warrants repeat imaging. Published cases document methotrexate exposure after mistaken ectopic-pregnancy diagnosis; accordingly, do not administer it at the first visit unless ectopic pregnancy is certain and viable intrauterine pregnancy has been excluded.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.3 Expectant management
document_sections.content: Observation is reasonable for selected, counselled women who can attend follow-up, have little pain and have low or declining serum b-hCG. Reported success ranges from 57–100%, strongly influenced by selection (Evidence level 3). Higher starting b-hCG corresponds to lower success. One study reported 96% success with b-hCG less than 175 iu/l and 66% with 175–1500 iu/l; other studies reported 80–90% when b-hCG was less than 1000 iu/l and 60–67% when it was less than 2000 iu/l. In a prospective observational study of tubal pregnancy, over 30% could be successfully observed: 146/333 underwent expectant management, with 71.2% (104/146) success. Selection required clinical stability without abdominal pain, no significant haemoperitoneum on ultrasound, mean ectopic diameter less than 30 mm, no embryonic heartbeat, serum b-hCG less than 1500 iu/l and patient consent. Follow-up continued until b-hCG was less than 20 iu/l, with individualised repeat-test intervals of 2 to 7 days. Observation stopped if the woman withdrew, developed significant pain, or had sustained b-hCG increase or a rise to greater than 2000 iu/l (Evidence level 2+). Another study proposed the pretreatment b-hCG ratio at 48 hours/0 hours: a ratio less than 0.8 predicted likely expectant-management success; overall success in that study was 72%. A multicentre RCT compared single-dose systemic methotrexate with observation in women with ectopic pregnancy or PUL and low or plateauing b-hCG—less than 1500 iu/l for ectopic pregnancy and less than 2000 iu/l for PUL. It found no difference in primary treatment success: 31/41 (76%) versus 19/32 (59%), respectively. Most participants, however, had PUL; only 15 (15/73; 21%) had visualised ectopic pregnancies (Evidence level 1+).

document_sections.heading: 5.2 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for cervical pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Consider methotrexate (D); reserve surgical approaches, which have high failure rates, for life-threatening bleeding (D). Early accurate diagnosis is central to conservative care. Gestation less than 12+0 weeks, absent fetal cardiac activity and lower serum b-hCG are associated with greater conservative-treatment success (Evidence level 2–). Described treatments include dilatation and curettage, systemic methotrexate and local potassium chloride or methotrexate injection. A retrospective review of 62 cases estimated approximately 91% efficacy for systemic methotrexate, but protocols varied and successful cases also needed surgical debulking or local methotrexate. Gestation more than 9+0 weeks, b-hCG greater than 10 000 iu/l, crown–rump length greater than 10 mm and fetal cardiac activity increased primary systemic-treatment failure risk; intra-amniotic combination treatment seemed to improve success in that review (Evidence level 2–). Haemorrhage-control adjuncts include uterine artery ligation and uterine artery embolisation (UAE). Small case series describe success when combined with intracervical or systemic methotrexate, but report infection, uterine infarction, sciatic-nerve injury, and bladder or rectal necrosis. Traditionally, dilatation and curettage required bleeding-control measures; because excessive bleeding requiring hysterectomy was frequent, restrict it to women for whom alternatives are unsuitable (Evidence level 3). A small series of five women treated by hysteroscopic resection and UAE reported no need for transfusion or additional techniques, but UAE has complications and long-term follow-up was unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for caesarean scar pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Counsel women about serious maternal morbidity and mortality (D). In first-trimester scar pregnancy, consider medical or surgical intervention, with or without additional haemostasis (D). Evidence is insufficient to prefer a particular intervention, although current literature suggests surgery is more effective than medical treatment (D). Among 35 first-trimester-diagnosed ongoing scar pregnancies continued by choice, reports describe 27 live births and 22 emergency hysterectomies at 15 to 38 weeks owing to haemorrhage and morbidly adherent placenta (Evidence level 3). Other small series and case reports describe abdominal rupture and severe vaginal bleeding at diagnosis or following intervention. A 2006–08 report recorded six haemorrhagic maternal deaths among women with previous caesarean section, without consistently establishing implantation location. Randomised treatment studies are few and small; most evidence comprises case series and reviews, including one systematic review limited to studies of five or more patients. Medical therapy uses ultrasound-guided intrasac or intramuscular systemic methotrexate; local injection appears more effective for ending the gestation. Remaining trophoblast may bleed as highly vascular placental tissue degenerates, prompting some authors to advocate suction evacuation alongside methotrexate. Surgical approaches include suction or hysteroscopic evacuation and open, laparoscopic or transvaginal excision. Suction evacuation is probably most frequently described, sometimes combined with cervical cerclage, a Foley catheter or UAE for haemostasis. Excision permits scar repair but is harder and more invasive; whether repair prevents later scar pregnancy or rupture is unknown. Observation may suit small, nonviable scar pregnancies. It may also be considered when implantation is partial and the pregnancy grows into the uterine cavity, provided the woman declines termination after counselling about haemorrhage and morbidly adherent placentation (Evidence level 3). Ongoing second-trimester scar pregnancy poses substantial maternal-morbidity and hysterectomy risk with any approach. Balance intervention against continuing toward potentially viable gestation; provide a care plan for morbidly adherent placenta and emergency action if rupture or haemorrhage occurs.

document_sections.heading: 5.4 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for interstitial pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Nonsurgical care is acceptable when stable (D). Reserve observation for low or markedly decreasing b-hCG where methotrexate might not improve outcome (D). Methotrexate is effective, but evidence cannot establish whether local or systemic administration is preferable (D). Laparoscopic cornual resection or salpingotomy is effective (D); hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic or ultrasound guidance is another possible technique (D). Insufficient information on future-pregnancy safety and complications prevents recommending other nonsurgical methods (D). Initial serum b-hCG influences conservative-treatment success. In a case series of 42 women, initial values were lower after successful expectant or medical care than after unsuccessful care (3216 iu/l versus 15 900 iu/l; P < 0.05). Another series of 19 expectantly managed women reported 89.5% success. One observational study of 17 women receiving systemic methotrexate 50 mg/m2 reported no complications; another reported adverse effects in 40% of recipients. An Australian series of 13 pregnancies reported 91% success with single-dose intravenous methotrexate plus oral folinic acid rescue. Described local treatment includes ultrasound-guided aspiration of gestational-sac exocoelomic fluid followed by intrasaccular 25 mg methotrexate, with or without 0.2–0.4 mEq potassium chloride. Reported success is 91%, with fewer adverse effects and an option for simultaneous embryocide, but the technique is more demanding; embryocide has been reported to increase procedural success (Evidence level 3). Reported endoscopic approaches include electrocautery, an endoloop or encircling suture before evacuation. Moon et al. described haemostasis using 1 ampoule [20 U] vasopressin in 1000 ml normal saline [1000-fold], injecting 150–250 ml [0.02 U/ml] below the pregnancy. Other reports describe laparoscopic haemostatic sutures and a ‘purse-string’ resection technique. Hysteroscopic resection under laparoscopic and ultrasound guidance has been reported. A small series (n = 3) described ultrasound-guided dilatation and evacuation with polypectomy forceps followed by single-dose systemic methotrexate. Selective UAE with methotrexate has been used to limit bleeding, but future-pregnancy safety and complications remain uncertain. A reported 12-week case after failed systemic methotrexate was treated successfully with intra-amniotic etoposide, described as a topoisomerase II inhibitor used for gestational trophoblastic disease (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 5.5 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for cornual pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Manage cornual pregnancy by laparoscopic or open excision of the rudimentary horn (D). Conservative, laparoscopic and open approaches have been described, including methotrexate and potassium chloride injection before later horn excision. Horn removal appears the best means of preventing recurrence. Laparoscopic excision is described as safe, but possible urinary-tract anomalies associated with a unicornuate uterus need attention. A reported technique divides the fibrous connection to the unicornuate uterus and removes the horn through a secondary port (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 5.6 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for ovarian pregnancy?
document_sections.content: If laparoscopy is needed to establish the diagnosis, prefer definitive surgery (D). Systemic methotrexate can be used when surgical risk is high or postoperatively for persistent residual trophoblast or persistently raised b-hCG (D). Minimally invasive surgery is the preferred approach. Remove conception products by enucleation, or by wedge resection when the ectopic lesion is large. Blunt ovarian enucleation limits injury to adjacent tissue; electrocautery or suturing can provide haemostasis. Oophorectomy is occasionally required for ipsilateral ovarian disease or excessive bleeding (Evidence level 3). Published methotrexate attempts have succeeded and failed; one series found 40% failure with methotrexate alone, and every successfully treated case in that series had been diagnosed laparoscopically. Defined selection, treatment and surveillance protocols are unavailable.

document_sections.heading: 5.7 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for abdominal pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Laparoscopic removal is an option in early abdominal pregnancy (D); systemic methotrexate with ultrasound-guided fetocide is a possible alternative (D). Use laparotomy for advanced pregnancy (D). Early laparoscopy can be safe and effective when implantation does not involve a vascular area; compared with laparotomy, reports associate it with less operative time and blood loss and shorter admission. Nonsurgical early-treatment reports are very few and include intramuscular methotrexate alone or combined with intrasaccular methotrexate. Methotrexate has also been described as a surgical adjunct. Advanced abdominal pregnancy has substantial maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality; once identified, undertake laparotomy promptly. Plan entry to avoid cutting through the placenta. If attached to major vessels or vital organs, it may be left in place for spontaneous resorption. Placental retention carries substantial risks of ileus, bowel obstruction, fistula, haemorrhage and peritonitis, but lower mortality than removal. Methotrexate and selective arterial embolisation have been described as adjuncts (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 5.8 What are the surgical, pharmacological or conservative treatment options for heterotopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Account for the intrauterine pregnancy and the woman’s wishes in the treatment plan (B; supporting Evidence level 2++). Consider methotrexate only when the intrauterine pregnancy is nonviable or the woman does not want to continue it (D). Methotrexate is not an option when a viable intrauterine pregnancy is intended to continue: even local injection can affect it. If a woman does not wish to continue a viable gestation, Abortion Act regulations apply (Evidence level 4). For clinically stable women, local potassium chloride or hyperosmolar glucose injection together with aspiration of the ectopic sac is an option (D). Hyperosmolar glucose is injected into the extrauterine sac; potassium chloride can be injected into the fetal pole when possible, otherwise into the sac. This may reduce surgical risks to the intrauterine pregnancy. Confirm ectopic resolution by ultrasound because b-hCG cannot be used for this purpose. The approach has been described for interstitial, caesarean scar and cervical heterotopic pregnancy (Evidence level 3). Surgical ectopic removal is the preferred approach in haemodynamic instability and remains an option in stable women (D), particularly with readily accessible tubal, cervical or interstitial ectopic pregnancy. During laparoscopy, avoid uterine cannulation or manipulation. Expectant management is an option when ultrasound indicates a nonviable ectopic pregnancy (D); reports include symptom-free women with an interstitial heterotopic pregnancy that ultrasound showed was not ongoing.

document_sections.heading: 6. Do rhesus D (RhD)-negative women with an ectopic pregnancy require anti-D immunoglobulin?
document_sections.content: Offer anti-D according to national protocol to RhD-negative women after operative removal of ectopic pregnancy or when bleeding is recurrent, heavy or accompanied by abdominal pain (D). Alloimmunisation has followed ectopic pregnancy, and 25% of ruptured tubal cases have a significant quantity of fetal cells in maternal blood (Evidence level 2–). No studies have assessed anti-D prophylaxis specifically in women with ectopic pregnancy. Surgery may raise sensitisation risk by mixing fetal and maternal blood. Evidence for alloimmunisation with medical or expectant care is sparse; mixing after these approaches is thought uncommon. NICE recommends prophylaxis only after surgery, unlike British Committee for Standards in Haematology guidance (Evidence level 4).

document_sections.heading: 7. What are the long-term fertility prospects following an ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Without previous subfertility or tubal disease, counsel that treatment methods do not differ in fertility, subsequent tubal ectopic-pregnancy risk or tubal patency (D). With prior subfertility, explain the association of expectant or medical care with better reproductive outcomes than radical tubal surgery (C). Advise that methotrexate for tubal pregnancy does not affect ovarian reserve (D); that live births after UAE plus systemic methotrexate for nontubal pregnancy have been reported (D); and that fertility prospects following ovarian-pregnancy laparoscopy are good (D). Comparative studies found no statistically significant difference in recurrent ectopic-pregnancy rates across surgical approaches or between surgical, medical and expectant care; most long-term reports give around 18.5% recurrence (Evidence level 1+). Hysterosalpingography found no difference in ipsilateral patency after expectant versus medical treatment, or contralateral patency after expectant, medical or surgical management (Evidence level 2–). In women with subfertility, particularly those over 35 years, radical surgery was associated with fewer subsequent intrauterine pregnancies than conservative surgery or medication. RCTs comparing medication with conservative or radical surgery, or conservative with radical surgery, found no difference in future fertility; other case series similarly found no difference between observation and radical surgery (Evidence level 1–). Studies of ovarian reserve after medical treatment found no effect on antim€ullerian hormone, antral follicle counts or ovarian responsiveness. A small study suggested fewer oocytes when fertility treatment resumed within 180 days after methotrexate. In a small series after UAE and systemic methotrexate for nontubal pregnancy, 12 women tried to conceive; 83% conceived and 58% had a live birth (Evidence level 3). Another small series after laparoscopic ovarian-pregnancy surgery reported 100% subsequently conceived and 83% had a live birth.

document_sections.heading: 8. What support and counselling should be offered to women undergoing treatment for ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Whenever possible, explain the advantages and disadvantages of each treatment and involve women fully in choosing care (D). Provide information on access to patient support organisations, including the Ectopic Pregnancy Trust, and local bereavement counselling (D). Muscle-relaxation training may help those receiving methotrexate (C). Recommend waiting at least 3 months after methotrexate before attempting conception (D). Early-pregnancy loss can seriously affect a significant proportion of women, partners and families psychologically (Evidence level 2–). Record follow-up plans clearly in the early-pregnancy clinic discharge letter and provide written material about options, surveillance and local or national support. A study suggested little psychological-outcome difference between medical and surgical ectopic-pregnancy management (Evidence level 3). Around half of affected women have a significant grief reaction; those without a child score higher on a perinatal grief measure. Support may also benefit subsequent pregnancies, when anxiety about outcome is more likely. In an RCT, women receiving adjunctive muscle relaxation using the Bernstein and Borkovec technique during methotrexate care had less anxiety and better health-related quality of life at hospital discharge than controls without this adjunct (Evidence level 1–). Methotrexate manufacturers advise a 3-month preconception interval because the drug can remain in some organs and might affect a later pregnancy or fetus. A small cohort found a higher-than-expected major-malformation rate after conception within 3 months of exposure. Nonetheless, conception within that interval is not itself an indication for termination (Evidence level 2–).

document_sections.heading: 9. Service and training
document_sections.content: Services need timely specialist assessment, access to appropriate treatments, suitably trained staff and adequate surgical resources. Requirements for service organisation and individual competencies are specified below.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 What is the most appropriate setting for management of women with an ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Early-pregnancy providers should offer assessment 7 days a week, direct access following general-practitioner or accident-and-emergency referral, diagnostic and therapeutic algorithms, transvaginal imaging, and serum b-hCG testing (good practice point). Ensure women can access all suitable treatments, using clear referral pathways where local facilities cannot provide them (good practice point). Consistent with cited NICE and RCOG recommendations, suspected ectopic pregnancy should be managed in dedicated early-pregnancy clinics. Ideally, these are separately located, appropriately staffed and open daily, 7 days a week. If assessment within 24 hours cannot be arranged there, provide referral elsewhere for specialist clinical review and scanning, such as a gynaecology ward or accident and emergency with specialist gynaecological support (Evidence level 4). Laparoscopic salpingotomy is outside core gynaecological training; a survey suggested 51% of trainees lacked the necessary skill, supporting availability of senior staff trained across procedures. Because scar pregnancy is uncommon, diagnostically difficult and has multiple treatment choices, clinically stable affected women should receive multidisciplinary care from an experienced team.

document_sections.heading: 9.2 What are the training implications for those managing women with ectopic pregnancy?
document_sections.content: Surgeons treating ectopic pregnancy must have suitable training, equipment and trained theatre staff for laparoscopy (good practice point). Diagnostic ultrasound and ultrasound-guided needle-based medical treatment each require appropriately trained clinicians (good practice points). If a surgeon cannot perform all necessary operations, appropriately experienced assistance must be available when required (good practice point). Virtual-reality simulators may be used for salpingectomy training (D). Clinical staff should receive RCOG-curriculum or equivalent training in open and laparoscopic treatment, including safe monopolar and bipolar diathermy, and have efficient contemporary equipment (Evidence level 4). Ultrasound practitioners should complete the RCOG intermediate module on early-pregnancy complications or demonstrate equivalent preparation. The RCOG Advanced Training Skills Module in acute gynaecology and early pregnancy does not establish independent ultrasound-guided needle competence; operators should document relevant training and maintain records of cases and complications. Ideally the operating clinician can perform both salpingectomy and salpingotomy; otherwise on-call expertise should be available for alternative procedures and practical training. Studies report that virtual-reality simulation provides realistic practice for operations including salpingectomy (Evidence level 3).

document_sections.heading: 10. Recommendations for future research
document_sections.content: The guideline identifies research needs concerning anti-D in nontubal ectopic pregnancy; methotrexate for ovarian ectopic pregnancy; long-term fertility after nontubal treatment; diagnostic-test studies for interstitial and caesarean scar pregnancy; long-term behaviour of implantation at, in or into a caesarean scar; optimal scar-pregnancy treatment; validation of expectant management; new biomarkers predicting response to methotrexate or observation; psychological consequences of ectopic pregnancy and its treatment; and multidose versus single-dose methotrexate for nontubal ectopic pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: 11. Auditable topics
document_sections.content: Suggested audit targets are identification of tubal ectopic pregnancy at the initial scan (90%); a negative laparoscopy after ultrasound diagnosis of tubal pregnancy (0%); offering all relevant treatments (100%); laparoscopic treatment among women suitable for it (100%); methotrexate after a false-positive ectopic-pregnancy diagnosis (0%); nonemergency operations between 8 p.m and 8 a.m. (0%); and provision of support-group information (100%).

document_sections.heading: 12. Useful links and support groups
document_sections.content: The guideline directs readers to the Association of Early Pregnancy Units, the Ectopic Pregnancy Trust, Infertility Network UK, the Miscarriage Association and RCOG information for people experiencing ectopic pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: Appendix I: Explanation of guidelines and evidence levels
document_sections.content: The guideline presents systematically developed advice to support clinician and patient decisions, not an exclusive or prescriptive treatment course. Apply it in light of individual needs, institutional resources and constraints, and local populations; areas of clinical uncertainty may require more research. Its evidence classification defines 1++ as high-quality meta-analyses, systematic reviews of RCTs or RCTs with very low bias risk; 1+ as well-conducted studies of those types with low bias risk; and 1– as studies of those types with high bias risk. Level 2++ covers high-quality systematic reviews of case–control or cohort studies, or high-quality individual studies of those designs with very low confounding, bias or chance risk and high likelihood of causation. Level 2+ denotes well-conducted case–control or cohort studies with low confounding, bias or chance risk and moderate likelihood of causation; 2– denotes those with high risk and a significant possibility that the relationship is not causal. Level 3 comprises non-analytical studies such as case reports and series; 4 denotes expert opinion. Recommendation grade A requires at least one directly applicable 1++ meta-analysis, systematic review or RCT, or a directly applicable systematic review of RCTs or consistent body principally rated 1+. Grade B reflects consistent, directly applicable 2++ evidence or extrapolation from 1++ or 1+. Grade C reflects consistent, directly applicable 2+ evidence or extrapolation from 2++. Grade D reflects evidence level 3 or 4, or extrapolation from 2+. A ‘Good practice point’ indicates best practice based on the guideline-development group’s clinical experience.

document_sections.heading: Appendix II: Single-dose protocol for intramuscular methotrexate
document_sections.content: The protocol’s day-and-treatment table specifies serum b-hCG, U&E, LFTs, FBC and blood group assessment with intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 on day 1; serum b-hCG testing on days 4 and 7; repeat TVS and methotrexate 50 mg/m2 if the decrease over days 4–7 is less than 15% and medical-treatment criteria still apply; or weekly b-hCG measurements until less than 15 iu/l when the decrease over days 4–7 is greater than 15%. The final table row’s wording is incomplete in the document; the greater-than-15% branch is also stated in the main pharmacological-management text.

document_sections.heading: Appendix III: Contraindications to methotrexate
document_sections.content: Listed contraindications are haemodynamic instability, intrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, inability to comply with follow-up, known methotrexate sensitivity, chronic liver disease, pre-existing blood dyscrasia, active pulmonary disease, immunodeficiency and peptic ulcer disease.
